answer:
I built GHZ states of 2, 3, 4, and 5 qubits. Each circuit puts one qubit in a 50/50 superposition and then uses entangling gates to tie the other qubits to it. A perfect machine would give only two results: all zeros or all ones, about half the time each. I first sent the 4-circuit job to the free test device sirius:mock (job 01a16054-e2f0-70ff-9861-c3b34d2a62f8). It completed. The test device returns fixed placeholder counts, so its numbers only show that the job is valid. I then ran the same job once on the real sirius QPU with 100 shots per circuit (job 01a16055-61f8-77fc-8966-d99627f7ad43). The API reports 1.0 billed second for it.

On the real machine, the share of shots where all bits agree was 96% for 2 qubits, 85% for 3, 85% for 4, and 79% for 5. A perfect machine would score 100% at every size. The good shots still split roughly evenly between all zeros and all ones. For example, the 5-qubit circuit gave 41 all-zeros and 38 all-ones. That even split is the signature of a GHZ state.

The trend is that bigger entangled states lose more quality. Each extra qubit needs one more two-qubit gate and one more readout. Every gate and every readout has a small chance of error. A single error on any qubit breaks the all-agree pattern, so the errors add up as the state grows. The 3-qubit and 4-qubit scores came out equal. With only 100 shots, each score is uncertain by about 4 percentage points, so that tie is within normal sampling noise. The principle is that entanglement is fragile. Noise grows with the size of the entangled state, and that is the main reason large quantum computations need error correction.

Note: agreement only counts how often the bits match. It does not prove that the two outcomes were in a true quantum superposition. A test of the phase between the outcomes would be needed for that.
